items.title: Ligand Recognition by Receptors in Three Cell Types
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify which ligand each cell type is able to recognize, and state what the data show about the receptors of the three cell types.

(b) Explain, in terms of receptor structure, why the receptor proteins from liver cells bind ligand R but not ligand P, even though both ligands are peptides.

(c) A fourth cell type has no receptor for ligand P. Predict whether this cell type will respond to ligand P, and justify your prediction.
items.stimulus:
A researcher studies three cell types and three signaling molecules (ligands), P, Q and R. Ligands P and R are different peptides (small proteins). Ligand Q is a small nonpolar molecule. The researcher prepared extracts containing the receptor proteins from each cell type and measured how much of each ligand bound to the receptor proteins (relative units; 100 is the maximum binding). Readings of 5 or below are background and mean that the ligand did not bind.

Cell type | Ligand P | Ligand Q | Ligand R
Muscle cell | 92 | 0 | 3
Liver cell | 4 | 0 | 88
Skin cell | 2 | 85 | 1
items.answer:
(a) Muscle cells recognize ligand P (92), liver cells recognize ligand R (88), and skin cells recognize ligand Q (85); each cell type shows almost no binding to the other two ligands. The three cell types therefore have different receptors, and each receptor is specific to only one of the ligands.

(b) The ligand-binding domain of a receptor has a specific shape. The liver-cell receptor has a binding domain whose shape fits ligand R, so R binds (88). Ligand P is also a peptide but has a different structure that does not fit this domain, so P does not bind (4).

(c) The cell type will not respond to ligand P. Signaling begins when a receptor protein in the target cell recognizes the ligand. Without a receptor for P, the cell cannot receive the signal, so no signal transduction occurs.

criteria.text: Identifies the ligand recognized by each cell type: muscle cells recognize P, liver cells recognize R, and skin cells recognize Q.
criteria.evidence: Response pairs each cell type with the one ligand that shows high binding (muscle with P, liver with R, skin with Q).
criteria.fix: For each row, find the one ligand with high binding and pair it with that cell type.

criteria.text: States that the three cell types have different receptors, and that each receptor binds only one of the ligands.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the receptors differ between cell types and that each receptor is specific to one ligand.
criteria.fix: Compare rows: if each cell type binds a different ligand and almost no others, the receptors are different and specific.

criteria.text: Explains that the receptor's ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that matches ligand R but not ligand P, so P cannot bind.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the ligand-binding domain recognizes a specific ligand through its shape or structure, which fits R and does not fit P.
criteria.fix: Name the receptor feature involved: the ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that fits only its own ligand.
variants: binding site is specific to its ligand

criteria.text: Predicts that the cell type will not respond to ligand P, because without a receptor that recognizes P, the signal cannot be received and the signaling does not start.
criteria.evidence: Response predicts no response and states that recognition of the ligand by a receptor protein is required to begin signaling.
criteria.fix: Link response to reception: a signal can start a response only if a receptor in the target cell recognizes the ligand.

items.title: Surface and Intracellular Receptors for Two Signals
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify which signal binds to a receptor on the cell surface, and use the data to support your answer.

(b) Explain, using the structure of the plasma membrane, why signal X can reach its receptor but signal Y needs a receptor on the cell surface.

(c) Explain why the receptor for signal Y does not respond to signal X.
items.stimulus:
Cells in a tissue culture respond to two signaling molecules by turning on a set of genes. Signal X is a small, nonpolar molecule. Signal Y is a large, polar molecule. Researchers added each signal to the medium outside the cells and measured gene activation in relative units.

In two treatments, the researchers first added a blocker. The blocker binds to proteins on the outer surface of the plasma membrane, so that no ligand can bind to them. The blocker cannot enter the cell.

Treatment | Gene activation (relative units)
1. No signal | 1
2. Signal X added outside the cells | 85
3. Signal Y added outside the cells | 90
4. Blocker, then signal X added outside the cells | 83
5. Blocker, then signal Y added outside the cells | 2
items.answer:
(a) Signal Y binds a receptor on the cell surface. When the blocker, which acts only on proteins on the outer surface, was present, the response to signal Y dropped from 90 to 2, but the response to signal X stayed about the same (85 with no blocker, 83 with the blocker).

(b) Signal X is small and nonpolar, so it can pass through the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and bind a receptor inside the cell. Signal Y is large and polar, so it cannot cross the bilayer. It must bind a receptor in the plasma membrane, and that receptor relays the signal into the cell.

(c) A receptor's ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that fits its own ligand. The receptor for signal Y has a binding site that matches signal Y but not signal X, so X cannot bind to it or activate it.

criteria.text: Identifies signal Y as the signal that binds a receptor on the cell surface.
criteria.evidence: Response names signal Y (not signal X) as the signal whose receptor is on the cell surface.
criteria.fix: Decide which signal's response depends on a blocker that works only outside the cell; that signal's receptor is on the surface.

criteria.text: Supports the answer with the blocker data: the response to signal Y fell from 90 to 2 when the blocker, which acts only outside the cell, was present.
criteria.evidence: Response cites the loss of the response to signal Y (about 90 to about 2) when the blocker was present. A comparison with signal X may be included but is not required.
criteria.fix: Cite the values for signal Y with and without the blocker; a large drop shows its receptor is reachable by the outside-only blocker.

criteria.text: Explains that signal X is small and nonpolar, so it can pass through the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer and bind a receptor inside the cell.
criteria.evidence: Response links X being nonpolar to crossing the hydrophobic core of the membrane to reach an intracellular receptor.
criteria.fix: Tie polarity to the bilayer: small nonpolar molecules cross the hydrophobic core, so they can bind receptors inside the cell.

criteria.text: Explains that signal Y is large and polar, so it cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer and must bind a surface receptor, which then relays the signal into the cell.
criteria.evidence: Response states that Y cannot cross the membrane because it is large or polar, so it acts through a receptor in the plasma membrane.
criteria.fix: State why Y cannot cross: large polar molecules are blocked by the hydrophobic core, so they need a membrane receptor to relay the message.

criteria.text: Explains that the receptor's ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that fits signal Y but not signal X, so X cannot bind and activate it.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the receptor's binding site is specific, with a shape that matches only its own ligand.
criteria.fix: Name the receptor feature involved: the ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that matches only its own ligand.
variants: binding site is specific to its ligand

items.title: Cyclin-CDK Activity and a Drug That Stops Cells Before Mitosis
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe the relationship between cyclin concentration and CDK activity in the first table, and explain the relationship.

(b) Based on the second table, identify the stage of the cell cycle at which most drug-treated cells are stopped, support your answer with values from the table, and explain what this shows about the role of the cyclin-CDK complex that the drug blocks.

(c) Cells with damaged DNA normally pause at an internal checkpoint. Explain how this pause benefits the organism.
items.stimulus:
Cyclins are proteins whose concentration changes during the cell cycle. A cyclin binds to a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK), and a CDK is active only when it is bound to a cyclin. Researchers followed a synchronized culture of dividing cells through one cell cycle and measured the concentration of the cyclin that regulates entry into mitosis and the activity of its partner CDK. Mitosis ended near hour 11.

Time (hours) | Cyclin concentration (relative units) | CDK activity (relative units)
0 | 5 | 4
3 | 20 | 18
6 | 55 | 52
9 | 90 | 88
12 | 8 | 6

The researchers then treated a second culture with a drug that blocks the active cyclin-CDK complex needed to enter mitosis. After 24 hours they measured the DNA content of each cell. A G1 cell has the 2C amount of DNA, and a cell that has finished DNA replication has 4C. They also counted cells with visible condensed chromosomes (cells in mitosis).

Group | % of cells in G1 (2C DNA) | % of cells in S phase (between 2C and 4C) | % of cells with 4C DNA (G2 or mitosis) | % of all cells in mitosis
Control culture | 48 | 22 | 30 | 4
Drug-treated culture | 8 | 12 | 80 | 0.4
items.answer:
(a) CDK activity rises and falls together with cyclin concentration: both are highest at 9 hours (90 and 88) and low at 0 and 12 hours. This is because a CDK is active only when it is bound to a cyclin, so the amount of active CDK depends on the amount of cyclin.

(b) Most drug-treated cells are stopped in G2. In the treated culture 80% of cells have 4C DNA, which means they have replicated their DNA, but only 0.4% are in mitosis (4% in the control). The active cyclin-CDK complex that the drug blocks is therefore needed for cells to pass the checkpoint from G2 into mitosis. Without it, cells cannot progress.

(c) When DNA is damaged, the checkpoint pauses the cycle. This gives the cell time to repair the DNA before it divides, so damaged DNA is not copied and passed to the daughter cells.

criteria.text: Describes that CDK activity rises and falls together with the cyclin concentration (both are highest at 9 hours and low at 0 and 12 hours).
criteria.evidence: Response states that CDK activity follows the cyclin concentration over time.
criteria.fix: Compare the two columns over time: when one rises or falls, state whether the other changes in the same direction.

criteria.text: Explains that CDK is active only when it is bound to cyclin, so CDK activity depends on the cyclin concentration.
criteria.evidence: Response states that cyclin binding is required to activate the CDK.
criteria.fix: Use the information given about the proteins: a CDK needs a bound cyclin to be active, so its activity tracks cyclin level.

criteria.text: Identifies G2 (after DNA replication and before mitosis) as the stage where most treated cells are stopped, supported by 80% of cells having 4C DNA while only 0.4% are in mitosis.
criteria.evidence: Response names G2 (or the point just before mitosis) and cites the large share of 4C cells and the very small share of cells in mitosis.
criteria.fix: Combine two clues: cells with 4C DNA have replicated their DNA, and few cells in mitosis means they stopped before mitosis.

criteria.text: Explains that the active cyclin-CDK complex is needed for cells to pass the checkpoint into mitosis, so blocking it keeps cells from progressing out of G2.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the cyclin-CDK complex is required for cells to move from G2 into mitosis.
criteria.fix: Connect the drug to the stop: if blocking the complex halts the cycle, then the active complex is required to move forward.

criteria.text: Explains that the pause gives the cell time to repair the damaged DNA, or keeps a cell with damaged DNA from dividing, so damaged DNA is not passed to daughter cells.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the checkpoint holds the cycle so repair can occur, or that it stops damaged cells from dividing, preventing passage of damaged DNA.
criteria.fix: State what the pause achieves: damaged DNA is repaired, or the damaged cell does not divide, so daughter cells do not inherit it.

items.title: A Checkpoint Mutation and the Response to DNA Damage
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe how the normal cells (cell line N) responded to UV exposure, using the data to support each response you describe.

(b) Explain how the mutation in cell line M changes the way those cells respond to UV exposure.

(c) Predict one long-term consequence for a person whose skin cells carry this mutation and are exposed to UV light repeatedly. Justify your prediction.
items.stimulus:
Cell line N is a normal line of skin cells. Cell line M has a mutation in a gene for a protein that normally detects DNA damage and stops the cell cycle before DNA replication (before S phase). Researchers exposed samples of each cell line to ultraviolet (UV) light, which damages DNA, and compared them with unexposed samples. Over the next 24 hours they measured the percentage of cells that entered S phase and the percentage of cells that underwent apoptosis (programmed cell death).

Cell line | UV exposure | % of cells entering S phase | % of cells undergoing apoptosis
N | none | 30 | 2
N | UV | 4 | 35
M | none | 31 | 2
M | UV | 29 | 3
items.answer:
(a) Normal cells stopped progressing through the cell cycle after UV exposure: the percentage entering S phase fell from 30% to 4%, which fits a checkpoint halting the cycle in response to DNA damage. Normal cells also underwent apoptosis much more often after UV exposure: from 2% to 35%.

(b) Cell line M has a mutation in the protein that detects DNA damage and stops the cycle, so its checkpoint does not work. After UV exposure, 29% of the M cells still entered S phase, nearly the same as without UV (31%), and only 3% underwent apoptosis. The damaged cells are neither held at the checkpoint nor removed.

(c) Cells with damaged DNA would keep dividing, so mutations would build up in the daughter cells. Because the cell cycle is no longer controlled by the checkpoint, cells could divide in an uncontrolled way and form a tumor, so the person would have a higher risk of skin cancer.

criteria.text: Describes that UV exposure caused cells to stop entering S phase (30% without UV, 4% with UV), consistent with a checkpoint halting the cycle.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the percentage of cells entering S phase fell sharply after UV exposure, and gives the values.
criteria.fix: Compare UV with no UV for the column that shows cell cycle progress, and give both values.

criteria.text: Describes that UV exposure caused many more cells to undergo apoptosis (2% without UV, 35% with UV).
criteria.evidence: Response states that apoptosis increased after UV exposure, and gives the values.
criteria.fix: Compare the apoptosis column for UV and no UV, and state the increase using both values.

criteria.text: Explains that the mutated protein does not detect DNA damage or stop the cycle, so the checkpoint fails and cells with damaged DNA keep entering S phase (29%) and rarely undergo apoptosis (3%).
criteria.evidence: Response states that the checkpoint fails in cell line M, so cells continue through the cycle with damaged DNA and apoptosis does not rise.
criteria.fix: State what the lost protein did in cell line N, then show that the data from M have lost that response.

criteria.text: Predicts that damaged cells keep dividing, mutations accumulate, and uncontrolled cell division can lead to a tumor or cancer.
criteria.evidence: Response predicts cancer or tumor formation and links it to cells dividing with damaged DNA that is not repaired or removed by apoptosis.
criteria.fix: Connect failed checkpoints to cancer: cells divide with damaged DNA, mutations accumulate, and division can become uncontrolled.

items.title: Confidence Interval for the Mean Length of Rainbow Trout
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Check the conditions for constructing a t interval for the population mean length.

(b) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean length of all rainbow trout in the lake.

(c) Interpret the interval in the context of the study.
items.stimulus:
A fisheries biologist wants to estimate the mean length of rainbow trout in a large lake that holds many thousands of trout. She catches and measures a random sample of 22 trout. The sample mean length is 31.4 cm and the sample standard deviation is 4.2 cm. A dotplot of the 22 lengths is roughly symmetric, with no outliers.

For 95% confidence with 21 degrees of freedom, the critical value is t* = 2.080.
items.answer:
(a) Random: the 22 trout are a random sample from the lake. 10% condition: the lake holds many thousands of trout, which is more than 10 × 22 = 220, so the 10% condition is met. Sample data: n = 22 is less than 30, but the dotplot is roughly symmetric with no outliers, so it is reasonable to use a t interval.

(b) Standard error = 4.2/√22 ≈ 0.895 cm. Margin of error = 2.080 × 0.895 ≈ 1.86 cm. The interval is 31.4 ± 1.86, or (29.54, 33.26) cm.

(c) I am 95% confident that the interval from 29.54 cm to 33.26 cm captures the true mean length of all rainbow trout in the lake.

criteria.text: States that the trout were randomly selected, which meets the random condition.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the sample is a random sample of the trout in the lake.
criteria.fix: Name the sampling method given in the problem and say that it meets the random sampling condition.

criteria.text: States that the 10% condition is met because the lake holds more than 10 × 22 = 220 trout.
criteria.evidence: Response compares the population size to 10 times the sample size, 220, and concludes the 10% condition is satisfied.
criteria.fix: Compare the population size to 10 times the sample size; if the population is larger, the 10% condition is met.

criteria.text: States that although n = 22 is less than 30, the sample is roughly symmetric with no outliers, so the sample data condition is met.
criteria.evidence: Response notes n is below 30 and uses the symmetric shape and absence of outliers to justify using t procedures.
criteria.fix: When n is under 30, describe the sample's shape: no strong skewness and no outliers supports using a t interval.

criteria.text: Sets up the interval as 31.4 ± 2.080(4.2/√22), with the sample mean, t*, s and n correctly substituted (the standard error is about 0.895 cm).
criteria.evidence: Response shows the t interval expression with 31.4, 2.080, 4.2 and 22 correctly substituted, or an equivalent calculator setup that names the same values.
criteria.fix: Write the interval as the sample mean plus or minus t* times s over the square root of n, then substitute each value.

criteria.text: Gives the interval 31.4 ± 1.86, or (29.54, 33.26) cm.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the interval as limits near 29.54 and 33.26 cm, or as 31.4 ± 1.86 cm.
criteria.fix: Add and subtract the margin of error from the sample mean, and write both limits with units.

criteria.text: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 29.54 to 33.26 cm captures the true mean length of all rainbow trout in the lake.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the confidence level, the interval, the parameter as a population mean, and the context of trout in the lake.
criteria.fix: Use the pattern: I am 95% confident the interval from a to b contains the true mean of the population described.

items.title: Confidence Interval for a Mean Change in Quiz Scores
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain why the teacher should analyze the 14 differences with a one-sample t procedure instead of treating the before scores and the after scores as two independent samples.

(b) Define the parameter of interest and construct a 90% confidence interval for it.

(c) Interpret the interval in context, and interpret the confidence level.
items.stimulus:
A teacher wants to estimate the mean change in quiz scores when students use a review app. She randomly selects 14 of the 1,150 students at her school. Each student takes a quiz on a topic, studies the topic with the app for a week, and then takes a different quiz of equal difficulty on the same topic. For each student she computes the difference d = (score after) − (score before).

The 14 differences have a mean of 3.9 points and a standard deviation of 5.1 points. Their distribution has no strong skewness and no outliers.

For 90% confidence with 13 degrees of freedom, the critical value is t* = 1.771.
items.answer:
(a) Each student takes a quiz before and after using the app, so the before and after scores for a student are paired and are not independent. The teacher should compute each student's difference and use a one-sample t interval on those 14 differences.

(b) Let μd be the true mean difference (score after − score before) in quiz scores for all students at the school. The interval is 3.9 ± 1.771(5.1/√14) = 3.9 ± 2.41, which is approximately (1.49, 6.31) points.

(c) I am 90% confident that the interval from 1.49 to 6.31 points captures the true mean change (after − before) in quiz scores for all students at the school. If she repeated this process many times, about 90% of the intervals constructed this way would capture the true mean difference.

criteria.text: Explains that each student provides both a before score and an after score, so the two sets of scores are paired (not independent), and analyzing the differences accounts for the pairing.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the data are matched pairs because each student is measured twice, and that the differences are analyzed as one sample.
criteria.fix: Check whether the same individuals appear in both sets of data; if so, the data are paired and you analyze the differences.

criteria.text: Defines μd as the true mean difference (score after − score before) in quiz scores for all students at the school.
criteria.evidence: Response defines the parameter as a population mean difference, states the order of subtraction, and states the population of students.
criteria.fix: Define the parameter as a population mean of the differences, with the direction of subtraction and the population named.
variants: μd = mean change in quiz score for all students at her school

criteria.text: Computes the interval 3.9 ± 1.771(5.1/√14), which is approximately (1.49, 6.31) points.
criteria.evidence: Response shows the t interval with correct values substituted, or a labeled one-sample t-interval calculation with the same inputs, and gives limits near 1.49 and 6.31.
criteria.fix: Use the mean of the differences, t*, and s divided by the square root of 14; then add and subtract the margin of error.

criteria.text: States that we are 90% confident that the interval from 1.49 to 6.31 points captures the true mean change (after − before) in quiz scores for all students at the school.
criteria.evidence: Response interprets the interval as capturing a population mean difference, in context, with the interval and 90% confidence stated.
criteria.fix: Interpret the interval by naming the parameter in context, including the direction of the difference and its units.

criteria.text: Interprets the confidence level: if the teacher repeated the sampling process many times, about 90% of the intervals constructed this way would capture the true mean difference.
criteria.evidence: Response describes the long-run proportion of intervals from repeated samples that capture the true parameter, with a value of about 90%.
criteria.fix: Describe the method, not one interval: in many repeated samples, about 90% of the intervals made this way capture the parameter.

items.title: Setting Up a Test About Mean Ambulance Response Time
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses for a test of the resident's belief, defining any parameter you use.

(b) Name the inference procedure that is appropriate for these hypotheses.

(c) The calls are a simple random sample. Verify the 10% condition and the sample data condition for using this procedure.
items.stimulus: A city's emergency services department states that the mean response time for ambulance calls is 8.0 minutes. A resident believes the true mean response time is longer. The resident obtains the department's records of about 5,400 calls from the past year and takes a simple random sample of 36 of those calls. The sample mean response time is 8.7 minutes and the sample standard deviation is 2.9 minutes. The distribution of the 36 response times is skewed to the right, with no extreme outliers.
items.answer:
(a) Let μ be the true mean response time, in minutes, for all ambulance calls in the city. H0: μ = 8.0 minutes. Ha: μ > 8.0 minutes.

(b) A one-sample t-test for a population mean is appropriate.

(c) 10%: there are about 5,400 calls, which is more than 10 × 36 = 360 (equivalently, 36 is less than 10% of 5,400), so the condition is met. Sample data: n = 36 is at least 30, so the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal even though the sample is skewed to the right.

criteria.text: Defines μ as the true mean response time (in minutes) for ambulance calls in the city (all calls, or the calls from the past year that were sampled).
criteria.evidence: Response defines the parameter as a population mean in context, naming ambulance calls in the city and the units of minutes; a restriction to the past year's calls is acceptable.
criteria.fix: Define the parameter in words: name it as a population mean and say which population it describes, with units.
variants: mean response time for the past year's ambulance calls

criteria.text: States the null hypothesis H0: μ = 8.0 minutes.
criteria.evidence: Response writes H0 with equality and the claimed value 8.0.
criteria.fix: Write H0 as the parameter equal to the value claimed by the department, 8.0 minutes.

criteria.text: States the alternative hypothesis Ha: μ > 8.0 minutes.
criteria.evidence: Response writes Ha with the greater-than sign, reflecting the resident's belief that the mean is longer.
criteria.fix: Match the direction of Ha to the belief: longer than 8.0 minutes means the parameter is greater than 8.0.

criteria.text: Identifies a one-sample t-test for a population mean.
criteria.evidence: Response names a one-sample t-test (or t-test for a mean), not a z-test and not a two-sample test.
criteria.fix: One quantitative variable from one sample with unknown population standard deviation calls for a one-sample t-test for a mean.

criteria.text: States that the 10% condition is met because the population of about 5,400 calls is more than 10 times the sample size of 36 (equivalently, 36 is less than 10% of 5,400).
criteria.evidence: Response compares 5,400 with 10 × 36 = 360, or 36 with 10% of 5,400 = 540, and concludes the condition is met.
criteria.fix: Compare the sample size with 10% of the population size, or the population size with 10 times the sample size, and state the conclusion.

criteria.text: Verifies the sample data condition: n = 36 is at least 30, so the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal even though the sample is skewed to the right.
criteria.evidence: Response states that n ≥ 30 justifies approximate normality of the sampling distribution despite skewness.
criteria.fix: Compare n with 30; when n is at least 30, skewness in the sample does not stop you from using t procedures.

items.title: Setting Up a Matched-Pairs Test for Caffeine Gum and 5 km Times
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain why a matched-pairs procedure is appropriate here instead of a two-sample procedure.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses for the scientist's test, defining any parameter you use.

(c) Verify the conditions for using a matched-pairs t procedure.
items.stimulus:
A sports scientist wants to know whether chewing caffeine gum before a 5 km run reduces the mean running time. She recruits 15 volunteer runners. Each runner completes two 5 km time trials one week apart, once after chewing caffeine gum and once after chewing placebo gum. For each runner, the order of the two conditions is assigned at random.

For each runner she records d = (time after placebo gum) − (time after caffeine gum), in seconds, so a positive d means the runner was faster with caffeine. The 15 values of d have a mean of 14 seconds and a standard deviation of 21 seconds. The distribution of the 15 values of d is roughly symmetric, with no outliers.
items.answer:
(a) Every runner completes the 5 km trial under both conditions, so the times with caffeine and the times with placebo are paired and are not independent. The scientist should analyze the 15 differences d as a single sample.

(b) Let μd be the true mean difference (placebo time − caffeine time), in seconds, in 5 km time for all runners like these volunteers. H0: μd = 0. Ha: μd > 0.

(c) Random: the order of the conditions was randomly assigned for each runner. Sample data: n = 15 is less than 30, but the differences are roughly symmetric with no outliers, so it is reasonable to use a t procedure.

criteria.text: Explains that each runner is measured under both conditions, so the two sets of times are paired (dependent), and the differences d form one sample to analyze.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the same runners appear in both conditions, so the data are paired and the differences are analyzed as one sample.

items.title: Sampling Distribution of the Difference in Mean Bag Weights
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) What is the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2?

(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2.

(c) Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2, and justify your answer.

(d) Suppose the inspector increases the sample from Machine 2 to 60 bags and keeps 36 bags from Machine 1. Calculate the new standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2, and state whether it is smaller than, larger than, or the same as before.
items.stimulus:
Two machines fill bags of rice. Machine 1 fills bags with a mean weight of μ1 = 502 g and a standard deviation of σ1 = 6 g. Machine 2 fills bags with a mean weight of μ2 = 500 g and a standard deviation of σ2 = 5 g. The shapes of the two distributions of bag weights are not known.

An inspector takes an independent random sample of n1 = 36 bags from Machine 1 and an independent random sample of n2 = 30 bags from Machine 2, and computes the difference in the sample means, x̄1 − x̄2. Each machine fills at least 5,000 bags in a day.
items.answer:
(a) The mean is μ1 − μ2 = 502 − 500 = 2 g.

(b) The standard deviation is √(6²/36 + 5²/30) = √(1 + 0.8333) ≈ 1.354 g.

(c) The sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is approximately normal. Both sample sizes, 36 and 30, are at least 30, so the central limit theorem applies to each sample mean and the difference is approximately normal even though the shapes of the populations are not known.

(d) The new standard deviation is √(6²/36 + 5²/60) = √(1 + 0.4167) ≈ 1.190 g. This is smaller than 1.354 g, because a larger sample size reduces the variability of the sample mean.

criteria.text: States that the mean of the sampling distribution is μ1 − μ2 = 502 − 500 = 2 g.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the mean as 2 g, found by subtracting the two population means in the order x̄1 − x̄2.
criteria.fix: The mean of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is the difference of the population means, taken in the same order.

criteria.text: Calculates the standard deviation as √(6²/36 + 5²/30) ≈ 1.354 g.
criteria.evidence: Response adds the two variances of the sample means before taking the square root, and gives a value near 1.35 g.
criteria.fix: Add σ1²/n1 and σ2²/n2 first, then take the square root; do not subtract or add standard deviations directly.

criteria.text: States that the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is approximately normal.
criteria.evidence: Response states the shape is approximately normal.
criteria.fix: State the shape of the sampling distribution of the difference, not of the population distributions.

criteria.text: Justifies the shape because both sample sizes (36 and 30) are at least 30, so the sampling distribution is approximately normal regardless of the population shapes.
criteria.evidence: Response cites both n1 = 36 and n2 = 30 being at least 30 (central limit theorem) as the reason.
criteria.fix: When population shapes are unknown, check that both sample sizes are at least 30 before claiming a normal shape.

criteria.text: Calculates the new standard deviation √(6²/36 + 5²/60) ≈ 1.190 g.
criteria.evidence: Response gives a value near 1.19 g from the correct formula with n2 = 60.
criteria.fix: Replace n2 with 60 in the variance of the second sample mean, add the two variances, then take the square root.

criteria.text: States that the new standard deviation is smaller than the original 1.354 g.
criteria.evidence: Response compares the new value with 1.354 g and states that the new value is smaller.
criteria.fix: Compare the new value with the earlier one and say which is smaller; a larger sample gives a smaller value.

items.title: Sampling Distribution of the Difference in Mean Battery Life
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B.

(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B.

(c) Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B, and justify your answer even though both sample sizes are less than 30.

(d) A second lab tests the same sample sizes of 9 and 12 batteries but does not know the shape of either population. Can it assume that the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B is approximately normal? Explain.
items.stimulus:
A consumer lab compares two brands of rechargeable flashlight batteries. The battery life of Brand A is normally distributed with a mean of 18.0 hours and a standard deviation of 2.4 hours. The battery life of Brand B is normally distributed with a mean of 16.5 hours and a standard deviation of 3.0 hours.

The lab tests an independent random sample of 9 Brand A batteries and an independent random sample of 12 Brand B batteries, and computes the difference in the sample means, x̄A − x̄B.
items.answer:
(a) The mean is μA − μB = 18.0 − 16.5 = 1.5 hours.

(b) The standard deviation is √(2.4²/9 + 3.0²/12) = √(0.64 + 0.75) = √1.39 ≈ 1.179 hours.

(c) The sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B is normal. Both populations are normally distributed, so each sample mean is normally distributed for any sample size, and the difference of two independent normal variables is also normal. The small sample sizes (9 and 12) do not matter here.

(d) No. If the shapes of the populations are unknown, neither sample size is at least 30, so the central limit theorem cannot be used, and the populations are not known to be normal. The second lab cannot assume a normal sampling distribution.

criteria.fix: Subtract the population means in the same order as the sample means: Brand A minus Brand B.

criteria.fix: Add the two variances of the sample means, then take the square root of the sum.

items.title: Confidence Interval for the Difference in Mean Sleep Time
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Check the conditions for constructing a two-sample t interval for μ1 − μ2.

(b) Construct a 95% confidence interval for μ1 − μ2.

(c) Interpret the interval in context.
items.stimulus:
A researcher at a large university compares the nightly sleep of students who use a phone in bed and students who do not. About 9,000 students at the university use a phone in bed and about 6,000 do not. She takes an independent random sample of 45 students from the first group and 52 students from the second group, and records each student's mean nightly sleep (in hours) over a week.

Group 1 (phone in bed): n1 = 45, mean 6.8 hours, standard deviation 1.1 hours.
Group 2 (no phone in bed): n2 = 52, mean 7.3 hours, standard deviation 0.9 hours.

Technology gives about 85.1 degrees of freedom. For 95% confidence, the critical value is t* = 1.988.
items.answer:
(a) Random and independent: the students in each group were chosen by random sampling, and the two samples are independent of each other. 10%: 9,000 is more than 10 × 45 = 450 and 6,000 is more than 10 × 52 = 520. Sample data: both n1 = 45 and n2 = 52 are at least 30, so the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is approximately normal.

(b) Point estimate: 6.8 − 7.3 = −0.5 hours. Standard error: √(1.1²/45 + 0.9²/52) ≈ 0.206. Margin of error: 1.988(0.206) ≈ 0.41. The interval is −0.5 ± 0.41, which is approximately (−0.91, −0.09) hours.

(c) I am 95% confident that the interval from −0.91 to −0.09 hours captures the true difference in mean nightly sleep (students who use a phone in bed minus students who do not) among students at the university.

criteria.text: States that the two samples are independent random samples from the two groups.
criteria.evidence: Response states that each sample is random and that the two samples are independent of each other.
criteria.fix: Say how each sample was chosen and that the groups are independent samples.

criteria.text: States that the 10% condition is met in each group: 9,000 is more than 10 × 45 = 450 and 6,000 is more than 10 × 52 = 520.
criteria.evidence: Response compares each group's population size to 10 times its sample size.
criteria.fix: Check each group separately: its population size must be at least 10 times its sample size.

criteria.text: States that both sample sizes (45 and 52) are at least 30, so the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is approximately normal.
criteria.evidence: Response cites both sample sizes being at least 30 as satisfying the sample data condition.
criteria.fix: For two samples, check that both n1 and n2 are at least 30 before relying on approximate normality.

criteria.text: Calculates the standard error √(1.1²/45 + 0.9²/52) ≈ 0.206 hours.
criteria.evidence: Response shows a standard error near 0.206 hours computed from both sample variances and both sample sizes.
criteria.fix: Add s1²/n1 and s2²/n2, then take the square root of the sum.

criteria.text: Gives the interval (6.8 − 7.3) ± 1.988(0.206), which is approximately (−0.91, −0.09) hours.
criteria.evidence: Response uses −0.5 as the point estimate, in the order group 1 minus group 2, and gives limits near −0.91 and −0.09 hours.
criteria.fix: Multiply t* by the standard error for the margin of error, then add and subtract it from the point estimate.

criteria.text: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from −0.91 to −0.09 hours captures the true difference in mean nightly sleep (phone in bed minus no phone in bed) for the two groups of students at the university.
criteria.evidence: Response states the confidence level, the interval, the order of subtraction, and that the parameter is a difference in population mean sleep times.
criteria.fix: Interpret with the confidence level, the interval, the order of subtraction, and the two populations named.

items.title: Confidence Interval for the Difference in Mean Tomato Yield
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Check the conditions for constructing a two-sample t interval for μA − μB.

(b) Construct a 90% confidence interval for μA − μB.

(c) Interpret the interval in context.
items.stimulus:
A gardener randomly assigns 26 tomato plants of the same variety to two fertilizers: 12 plants receive fertilizer A and 14 plants receive fertilizer B. After 12 weeks she records the total mass of tomatoes (in kg) harvested from each plant. Dotplots of the yields in each group are roughly symmetric with no outliers.

Fertilizer A: n1 = 12, mean 4.60 kg, standard deviation 0.62 kg.
Fertilizer B: n2 = 14, mean 4.15 kg, standard deviation 0.75 kg.

Technology gives about 24.0 degrees of freedom. For 90% confidence, the critical value is t* = 1.711.
items.answer:
(a) Random: the 26 plants were randomly assigned to the two fertilizers, so the two groups are independent. Sample data: both sample sizes (12 and 14) are less than 30, but the yields in each group are roughly symmetric with no outliers, so it is reasonable to use a two-sample t interval.

(b) Point estimate: 4.60 − 4.15 = 0.45 kg. Standard error: √(0.62²/12 + 0.75²/14) ≈ 0.269. Margin of error: 1.711(0.269) ≈ 0.46. The interval is 0.45 ± 0.46, which is approximately (−0.01, 0.91) kg.

(c) I am 90% confident that the interval from −0.01 to 0.91 kg captures the true difference in mean tomato yield per plant (fertilizer A minus fertilizer B) for plants like these.

items.title: Using an Interval to Judge Claims About Puzzle Times with Music
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Does the interval provide convincing evidence of a difference in mean completion time between the two conditions? Justify your answer.

(b) Suppose that instead the interval had been (−6.2, −0.7) seconds. Would the interval provide convincing evidence of a difference in mean completion time? If so, state which condition has the lower mean. Justify both answers using the interval.

(c) A coach claims that music lowers the mean completion time by 6 seconds, that is, μmusic − μnone = −6. Does the original interval (−4.8, 1.9) support this claim? Explain.
items.stimulus: A psychologist randomly assigns 80 volunteers to solve the same puzzle, 40 with background music and 40 without music. She records each volunteer's completion time in seconds. Let μmusic − μnone be the true difference in mean completion time (music minus no music). A 95% confidence interval for μmusic − μnone is (−4.8, 1.9) seconds. The conditions for the interval were met.
items.answer:
(a) No. The interval (−4.8, 1.9) contains 0, so 0 is a plausible value for the true difference in mean completion time. There is not convincing evidence of a difference between the conditions.

(b) Yes. The interval (−6.2, −0.7) does not contain 0, so 0 is not a plausible value, and there would be convincing evidence of a difference. Every value in the interval is negative for music minus no music, so the mean completion time is lower with music.

(c) No. The claimed value −6 is not in the interval (−4.8, 1.9), so −6 is not a plausible value for the true difference. The interval does not support the coach's claim.

criteria.fix: Check whether 0 lies between the interval's limits; if it does, no difference is a plausible value.

criteria.evidence: Response concludes there is convincing evidence of a difference and cites that 0 is not in (−6.2, −0.7).
criteria.fix: If 0 is not in the interval, 0 is not a plausible value, so there is convincing evidence of a difference.

criteria.evidence: Response identifies music as having the lower mean and ties it to the interval containing only negative values of music minus none.
criteria.fix: Use the order of subtraction: if every value of music minus none is negative, the music mean is lower.

items.title: Using an Interval to Judge Claims About Two Teaching Methods
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Does the interval provide convincing evidence of a difference in mean exam score between the two methods? If so, state which method has the higher mean, and explain.

(b) A school board member claims that the true mean difference is exactly 5 points. Is the claim consistent with the interval? Does the interval establish that the claim is true? Explain.

(c) A principal claims that Method A gives a mean exam score that is more than 10 points higher than Method B, that is, μA − μB > 10. Does the interval support this claim? Explain.
items.stimulus: A school district randomly assigns 120 students to learn a unit with Method A and 120 students to learn it with Method B. Each student takes the same end-of-unit exam, scored out of 100. Let μA − μB be the true difference in mean exam score (Method A minus Method B). A 95% confidence interval for μA − μB is (2.1, 9.7) points. The conditions for the interval were met.
items.answer:
(a) Yes. The interval (2.1, 9.7) does not contain 0, so 0 is not a plausible value for the true difference, and there is convincing evidence of a difference in mean exam score. Every value in the interval is positive for A minus B, so Method A has the higher mean score.

(b) The claim is consistent with the interval because 5 is between 2.1 and 9.7, so 5 is a plausible value. The interval does not establish that the difference is exactly 5, because many other values in the interval, such as 3 or 8, are also plausible.

(c) No. The upper limit of the interval is 9.7, so every plausible value of μA − μB is less than 10. The interval does not support the claim that Method A is more than 10 points higher.

items.title: Setting Up a Test Comparing Mean GPA of On-Campus and Commuting Students
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses for the registrar's test, defining any parameters you use.

(b) Name the inference procedure that is appropriate for these hypotheses.

(c) The samples are independent random samples. Verify the 10% condition for each group and the sample data condition for using this procedure.
items.stimulus: A university registrar wants to know whether the mean GPA of students who live on campus differs from the mean GPA of students who commute. About 7,000 students live on campus and about 4,500 commute. She takes an independent random sample of 60 on-campus students and a separate independent random sample of 48 commuting students and records each student's GPA. The GPAs in each sample are not strongly skewed and there are no outliers.
items.answer:
(a) Let μ1 be the true mean GPA of all on-campus students at the university, and let μ2 be the true mean GPA of all commuting students at the university. H0: μ1 − μ2 = 0. Ha: μ1 − μ2 ≠ 0.

(b) A two-sample t-test for the difference between two population means is appropriate.

(c) 10%: 7,000 is more than 10 × 60 = 600, and 4,500 is more than 10 × 48 = 480, so the condition is met for both groups. Sample data: both sample sizes (60 and 48) are at least 30, so the sampling distribution of the difference in sample means is approximately normal.

criteria.evidence: Response defines both parameters as population means in context for the two groups.
criteria.fix: Define each parameter as a population mean and name which group it describes.

criteria.text: States the null hypothesis H0: μ1 − μ2 = 0 (equivalently μ1 = μ2).
criteria.evidence: Response writes H0 as no difference between the two population means.
criteria.fix: Write H0 as the two population means being equal, which is a difference of 0.

criteria.text: States the alternative hypothesis Ha: μ1 − μ2 ≠ 0 (equivalently μ1 ≠ μ2).
criteria.evidence: Response writes a two-sided Ha, because the registrar wants to know whether the means differ.
criteria.fix: Match Ha to the question: asking whether the means differ, with no direction, calls for a not-equal alternative.

criteria.text: Identifies a two-sample t-test for the difference between two population means.

criteria.text: States that the 10% condition is met in each group: 7,000 is more than 10 × 60 = 600 and 4,500 is more than 10 × 48 = 480.
criteria.evidence: Response compares each population size with 10 times the corresponding sample size (or each sample size with 10% of its population size).
criteria.fix: Check each group separately by comparing its sample size with 10% of its population size.

criteria.text: States that the sample data condition is met because both sample sizes (60 and 48) are at least 30, or because neither sample is strongly skewed and there are no outliers.
criteria.evidence: Response cites both n1 = 60 and n2 = 48 being at least 30, or the absence of strong skewness and outliers in both samples.
criteria.fix: Compare both sample sizes with 30; when both are at least 30, the sampling distribution of the difference is approximately normal.

items.title: Setting Up a Test for a New Recovery Drink in a Cycling Experiment
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain why a two-sample procedure is appropriate here instead of a matched-pairs procedure.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses for the scientist's test, defining any parameters you use.

(c) Verify the conditions for using a two-sample t procedure.
items.stimulus: A sports scientist wants to test whether a new recovery drink lowers the mean time needed to complete a 20 km cycling time trial. She randomly assigns 24 cyclists to two groups of 12, without matching them on any characteristic. Group 1 drinks the new recovery drink and Group 2 drinks the standard recovery drink after a hard workout. The next day, each cyclist rides a 20 km time trial, and the scientist records the time in minutes. The times in each group are roughly symmetric with no outliers.
items.answer:
(a) Each cyclist is in only one group and drinks only one of the two drinks, so the two groups are independent and there is no pairing between them. A two-sample procedure is appropriate.

(b) Let μ1 be the true mean 20 km time trial time, in minutes, for cyclists after the new recovery drink, and let μ2 be the true mean time for cyclists after the standard recovery drink. H0: μ1 − μ2 = 0. Ha: μ1 − μ2 < 0.

(c) Random: the 24 cyclists were randomly assigned to the two groups. Sample data: both sample sizes (12 and 12) are less than 30, but the times in each group are roughly symmetric with no outliers, so it is reasonable to use a two-sample t procedure.

criteria.text: Explains that there is no pairing: each cyclist is in only one group and was not matched with a cyclist in the other group, so the two groups are independent.
criteria.evidence: Response states that no individual is measured twice and no cyclists were matched across the groups, so the data are two independent samples.
criteria.fix: Check for pairing: the same individual measured twice, or deliberately matched individuals; if neither, use a two-sample procedure.

criteria.text: Defines the parameters in context: μ1 and μ2 as the true mean 20 km times (in minutes) after the new drink and the standard drink, or one parameter μ1 − μ2 as the true difference in mean times.
criteria.evidence: Response defines either both population means or their difference as population parameters in context, with the order of subtraction if a difference is used.
criteria.fix: Define each parameter as a true mean time for one treatment, or the difference of the two, in context with units.

criteria.text: States the null hypothesis H0: μ1 − μ2 = 0 (equivalently μ1 = μ2).
criteria.evidence: Response writes H0 as no difference between the two true mean times.
criteria.fix: Write H0 as the two true means being equal, which is a difference of 0.

criteria.text: States the alternative hypothesis Ha: μ1 − μ2 < 0 (equivalently μ1 < μ2).
criteria.evidence: Response writes Ha with a less-than sign, because the new drink is expected to lower the mean time.
criteria.fix: Match Ha to the claim: a lower mean time with the new drink means the first mean is less than the second.

criteria.text: States that the random condition is met because the cyclists were randomly assigned to the two groups.
criteria.evidence: Response states that random assignment of cyclists to the two drinks satisfies the random condition.
criteria.fix: In an experiment, the random condition is met by random assignment of subjects to treatments; state what was randomized.

criteria.text: States that both sample sizes (12 and 12) are less than 30, but the times in each group are roughly symmetric with no outliers, so the sample data condition is met.
criteria.evidence: Response notes both n are below 30 and uses the symmetric shape and absence of outliers in each group.
criteria.fix: When a sample size is under 30, check each group for strong skewness and outliers before using t procedures.
